```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(modelr)
library(glmnet)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(broom)
```

```{r generate-data}
set.seed(2024)
n <- 200; p <- 50
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
colnames(X) <- paste0("V", 1:p)
y <- 2 * X[, 1] - 1.5 * X[, 2] + rnorm(n)

data("diamonds", package = "ggplot2")
```

## Task 1: Fit Ridge and LASSO with cross-validation

```{r task1}
set.seed(42)  # for reproducibility of CV fold assignment
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
cv_ridge  <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, nfolds = 10)

plot(cv_lasso)
title("LASSO: CV-MSE vs log(lambda)", line = 2.5)

cat("LASSO lambda.min:  ", round(cv_lasso$lambda.min,  4), "\n")
cat("LASSO lambda.1se:  ", round(cv_lasso$lambda.1se,  4), "\n")
cat("Ridge lambda.min:  ", round(cv_ridge$lambda.min,  4), "\n")
cat("Ridge lambda.1se:  ", round(cv_ridge$lambda.1se,  4), "\n")
```

## Task 2: Extract and compare coefficients

```{r task2}
lasso_coef <- coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.1se")
ridge_coef <- coef(cv_ridge, s = "lambda.1se")

cat("LASSO non-zero coefficients at lambda.1se:\n")
print(lasso_coef[lasso_coef[,1] != 0, ])

cat("\nNumber of non-zero LASSO coefficients:",
    sum(lasso_coef[-1, ] != 0), "\n")  # exclude intercept
cat("Number of zero LASSO coefficients:    ",
    sum(lasso_coef[-1, ] == 0), "\n")

cat("\nRidge: any exactly zero coefficients?",
    any(ridge_coef[-1, ] == 0), "\n")

# LASSO correctly identifies V1 (≈ +2) and V2 (≈ −1.5) as the only
# non-zero predictors, setting the remaining 48 coefficients to exactly 0.
# Ridge keeps all 50 but shrinks them toward 0.
```

## Task 3: LASSO coefficient path

```{r task3}
lasso_path <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)

plot(lasso_path, xvar = "lambda",
     main = "LASSO coefficient paths")
abline(v = log(cv_lasso$lambda.1se), lty = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = "lambda.1se", lty = 2, col = "red")

# As lambda decreases (left to right), more coefficients enter the model.
# V1 and V2 (the true predictors) enter first and have the largest
# magnitude at any given lambda.
```

## Task 4: Decision tree on diamonds

```{r task4}
tree_mod <- rpart(
  price ~ carat + cut + color + clarity,
  data    = diamonds,
  control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 4, cp = 0.001)
)

rpart.plot(tree_mod, type = 4, extra = 101,
           main = "Regression tree: diamond price")

cat("\nVariable importance:\n")
print(tree_mod$variable.importance)

# The first split is always on carat — confirming it as the dominant
# predictor of price. Subsequent splits refine by clarity and color.
```

## Task 5: Compare tree RMSE to OLS RMSE

```{r task5}
# Tree predictions
tree_pred <- predict(tree_mod, diamonds)
tree_rmse <- sqrt(mean((diamonds$price - tree_pred)^2))

# OLS log-log model predictions (back-transformed)
mod_lm   <- lm(log(price) ~ log(carat) + cut + color + clarity, data = diamonds)
lm_pred  <- exp(predict(mod_lm, diamonds))
lm_rmse  <- sqrt(mean((diamonds$price - lm_pred)^2))

cat("Tree RMSE:", round(tree_rmse, 0), "USD\n")
cat("OLS RMSE: ", round(lm_rmse,  0), "USD\n")

# OLS has lower RMSE because:
# (1) The log-log model captures the continuous, smooth price-carat
#     relationship, while the tree only approximates it with step functions.
# (2) The tree with maxdepth = 4 has at most 2^4 = 16 leaf nodes —
#     very coarse — while OLS uses a single continuous formula.
# Trees shine when the relationship is genuinely piecewise-constant or
# when complex interactions among many predictors are present.
```
